It is demonstrated that ServiceX streamlines data delivery, simplifies tool usage, and enhances collaboration among researchers, ultimately reducing the need for extensive software frameworks and promoting scientific innovation. This work introduces EarthNets, a cloud-based platform for deep learning and remote sensing tasks, designed to facilitate the evaluation of various techniques by providing users with a comprehensive and user-friendly interface. Remote sensing data is pre-processed and stored within the platform, allowing for the assessment of different deep learning methods against a range of satellite image datasets. EarthNets is built using a cloud service framework, allowing users to create and configure deep learning pipelines, conduct experiments, and collaboratively analyze results, all while maintaining the benefits of working in the cloud. The platform is freely accessible to the public, and we outline its core capabilities and features through the perspective of several use cases that illustrate its value. We also highlight the benefits of EarthNets as a research tool and demonstrate its potential through examples related to crop type classification, crop monitoring, and vegetation cover estimation. Our evaluation reveals that EarthNets offers a standardized and efficient framework for deep learning experiments, making it an ideal tool for remote sensing applications. We envision that EarthNets will serve as a valuable resource for researchers, academia, and industry professionals who are seeking a cloud-based solution for remote sensing tasks, deep learning pipelines, and associated toolboxes. The platform is available at https://earthnets.cloud. We encourage interested users to explore EarthNets and contribute to its growth by providing feedback and potential contributions. Mobile Augmented Reality applications can significantly boost user engagement and interaction with mobile devices. However, these applications often consume excessive bandwidth, posing significant challenges to the network. To address this issue, we introduce a novel service decomposition and replication strategy, Service Decomposition and Replication for Mobile Augmented Reality (SDRMAR), which optimizes network resources and ensures a seamless user experience. By breaking down complex AR applications into smaller, manageable components, SDRAMAR enables efficient data caching and replication, accelerating processing and reducing latency. Additionally, the dynamic replication mechanism ensures data availability and accelerates processing according to network conditions. Through simulations using a network mobility model, the results demonstrate SDRAMAR's effectiveness in enhancing user experience and reducing resource consumption in mobile AR applications. Notably, the strategy achieves significant bandwidth savings of up to 90% for certain AR applications, making it an invaluable resource for mobile AR services. To validate the proposal, the SDRAMAR framework has been implemented in a real-world mobile AR platform, the Google AR Engine, and the results confirm its feasibility and effectiveness. Moreover, the study highlights the impact of network conditions on user engagement and interaction with mobile AR applications, providing valuable insights. A key challenge in developing unsupervised reinforcement learning methods is
their lack of evaluation due to the limited availability of unsupervised tasks
and the associated evaluation metrics. To address this issue, we introduce
the Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning Benchmark (URLB), a collection of
six tasks that can be controlled using deep reinforcement learning methods.
These tasks are categorized into two groups: those that utilize image data
and those that do not rely on image data. The tasks in URLB are designed to
evaluate the capabilities of different models, including those with various
architectures, and the same model when trained differently. Our results show
that the top-performing models exhibit significant overfitting when tested on
URLB tasks, thereby making this benchmark a valuable tool to assess and
compare the effectiveness of future unsupervised reinforcement learning
methods. The URLB dataset can be accessed at
https://github.com/isaialon/URLB. unpaired@cs.cmu.edu for further inquiries. 
A video showcasing the benchmark tasks is available at
https://youtu.be/8Dv3kZ3Zr3g. A companion paper has been published at

This research presents a deep learning solution for enhancing images obtained from low-light RAW data across various scenes, environments, and camera types. Building upon the success of recent studies, we introduce a novel deep learning framework that leverages a hybrid residual network architecture to effectively restore both visual details and overall appearance in low-light images derived from RAW data. Thoroughly evaluated and experimentally validated, our method consistently delivers superior results in multiple benchmarking tests, significantly outperforming existing approaches on a diverse range of low-light images. To promote further research, our project resources, including the trained model and source code, will be made publicly accessible soon. Our project webpage includes additional information at: http://www.vision.cs.columbia.edu/seita/LRRNet.

We introduce an innovative approach for analyzing spatio-temporal data by
segmenting it into logical groups of spatial locations at various moments. Our
method leverages the inherent relationships within the data to uncover a
flexible and comprehensive structure. We initiate the segmentation process
by using a hierarchical clustering technique to group similar time points
together and a graph-based method to connect similar locations across time.
Subsequently, we utilize this combined structure to identify clusters that
satisfy a user-defined logical formula. Our algorithm iteratively refines these
clusters by removing any groups that violate the specified formula, resulting
in a final structure that provides a concise summary of the spatio-temporal
data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through both artificial
and real-world examples, showcasing its ability to uncover complex structures
hidden within large datasets. Our results also indicate that our method
significantly outperforms existing approaches in terms of the number of
clusters identified and the accuracy of the analysis. We further validate the
usefulness of our method by applying it to a real-world case study involving
the monitoring of water quality in the Hudson River. Our analysis reveals
patterns of water pollution and identifies areas where our method can be
applied to inform policy decisions. We also present a comprehensive analysis of
the computational efficiency of our method, comparing its performance to
standard baseline methods. Our results show that our method achieves a
significant reduction in computational time, up to 10 times faster, for large
datasets. We release the code and datasets used in our experiments for public
access, along with a user-friendly interface for interactive segmentation
exploration. Our research provides a new framework for analyzing spatio-temporal

Nevertheless, the extent to which these networks maintain their original level of performance in response to specific types of perturbations remains unclear. To address this question, we have developed a metric known as the Robustness Ratio, which assesses the accuracy gain resulting from the removal of adversarial inputs, as opposed to the corresponding decrease in accuracy when clean inputs are subjected to attacks. Our experiments utilizing datasets such as CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, along with various attack methods, have shown that the Robustness Ratio effectively measures the trade-off between adversarial robustness and normal performance for different CNN models. Finally, the proposed Robustness Ratio can be employed to evaluate the efficacy of novel defense strategies and optimization methods designed to reduce the vulnerability of neural networks to adversarial attacks. This paper presents a novel, non-invasive method for accurately determining the orientation of an object in three-dimensional space using only audio recordings obtained from a single perspective. To validate our approach, we conducted an in-depth analysis using both simulated data and real-world recordings from a mobile device. Research suggests that humans divide complex tasks into smaller components for more efficient problem-solving, yet the exact mechanisms driving this process are unclear. Our study proposes a simplified cognitive model to explain task decomposition based on a cost-benefit analysis. According to this model, people balance the costs of planning, errors during execution, and the mental burden of memory retrieval. Our findings indicate that performance is influenced by both the difficulty of planning and the likelihood of memory errors. Specifically, performance is improved when the probability of memory errors is low, making it unnecessary to expend energy on memory retrieval during planning. Conversely, when the memory probability is high, performance is optimized by investing more energy in memory retrieval during planning. Notably, our results suggest that people adjust their planning strategies in accordance with the memory burden, rather than trying to minimize this cost. This new model provides a more comprehensive understanding of human task decomposition and highlights the importance of memory in this process. Our research contributes to the field of artificial intelligence by offering a more nuanced approach to decomposition, one that goes beyond mere error minimization. Instead, it proposes a cost-benefit framework that takes into account various trade-offs, including memory costs. Our findings have significant implications for the design of intelligent systems that must handle complex tasks that rely heavily on memory. We demonstrate that our cognitive model can be applied to a wide range of intelligent systems that operate within memory-constrained environments. Our approach can be used to optimize the decomposition of tasks in these systems, and we provide an example of how this can be achieved using a simple reinforcement learning algorithm. Our method has the potential to significantly improve the performance of intelligent systems that operate in these environments, as demonstrated by our experiments. The key benefit of our design is its ability to implement various types of neurons and enable the creation of network architectures with improved performance. The high node count and scalability of our design also allow for the creation of networks with a wide range of layer configurations, leading to improved performance. The successful implementation of this platform in a software framework has enabled the rapid prototyping of photonic neural networks, which can be efficiently designed, optimized, and fabricated. The results demonstrate the potential of our approach to accelerate the development and deployment of high-performance photonic neural networks in real-world applications. The source code for our software framework is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/photoniccomputing/PCNC. We introduce a pioneering framework called FOON that utilizes task trees to
generate recipes for common cooking tasks. Unlike previous research, our system
allows users to create recipes in a visual format by selecting the right recipe
ingredients and tools. To test our approach, we developed an interactive tool
for creating task trees and generated recipes for 20 popular cooking tasks.
We then compared the quality of our generated recipes to those found on a well-known
recipe website. The results showed that our recipes met the standards of
correctness, completeness, and cooking length for the majority of tasks.
Moreover, our system outperformed human-created recipes in terms of efficiency,
as it can process tasks 2.5 to 3 times faster within the first 10 minutes.
This suggests that FOON can be a valuable tool for generating recipes for human
use. We also envision using FOON to create a recipe planning system that can
aid humans in finding recipes and planning their cooking tasks. The code for
our system is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/lyricfiessler/FOON.

This study examines the application of differential privacy in achieving private machine learning. We compared the effectiveness of DP-AE, DP-AE2, DP-AE3, DP-AE4 and DP-AE5 algorithms against traditional techniques such as L1, L2 and Lasso regularization methods. Our experiments using the Boston dataset showed that DP-AE5 outperformed the regularization methods in terms of both privacy protection and model accuracy. We also found that as the noise level increases, the model accuracy initially improves before declining, indicating that a lower noise level is optimal for satisfactory privacy and accuracy. Moreover, our experiments revealed that DP-AE5 provides better protection against data poisoning attacks than the unprivate Boston housing dataset model. Our results suggest that DP-AE5 is a superior choice for achieving private machine learning. We expect that our findings will contribute to a deeper understanding of differential privacy and motivate further research in the field. We have developed an extended Tempored Lefschetz Thimble Method (TLT) that allows 
first-principles calculations to be expanded, thereby increasing their range of 
application in first-principles calculations. This method utilizes a higher 
dimensional space, called the worldvolume, to expand upon the tempered integration 
approach and includes an additional integration over worldvolume modes in the 
action. This modification enables the integration of non-hermitian fermion 
operators, such as those used in first-principles calculations, without requiring 
complex phase factor cancellations. Our method achieves this by implementing a 
simplified, efficient algorithm that eliminates the need for phase factor cancellations 
and instead relies on a worldvolume extension that can be optimized to prevent 
unwanted worldvolume mode contributions. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our 
method, we have applied it to a Kondo lattice model and a Hubbard model, showing 
that worldvolume modes have little to no impact on the results when the models are 
optimized correctly. This method holds great potential for expanding the scope of 
first-principles calculations to a wider range of systems. Moreover, our approach 
opens up new avenues for improving existing algorithms by exploring the integration 
of worldvolume modes into the Lefschetz thimble method. Finally, we have also 
demonstrated the feasibility of our expanded TLT method using a quantum computer, 
enabling the application of first-principles calculations to quantum computing 
platforms. Our work presents a significant step forward in the field of quantum 
computing and first-principles calculations. To facilitate further research, we 
have made our expanded TLT code publicly available online.

A key challenge arises from balancing the high computational requirements of traditional processing algorithms with the need for strict privacy protection. To address this, we employ Somewhat Homomorphic Encryption to securely transmit user data, limiting the service provider's knowledge to aggregated, encrypted information. A novel weighted generalised ranking algorithm is developed to be computationally efficient while adhering to encryption limitations. Additionally, our approach incorporates a new optimization technique to further enhance its speed and suitability for real-time processing. A comprehensive theoretical analysis is provided, along with experimental results confirming that our approach meets all performance standards while maintaining the required level of precision. Ultimately, this solution enables location-based services to protect users' confidentiality without compromising their privacy. Superconducting radio-frequency (SRF) cavities are a crucial component of modern, powerful accelerators such as the LHC, but they are susceptible to degradation due to quenching, which can be triggered by resonant noise. This paper outlines a comprehensive setup for noise control and demonstrates the effectiveness of these techniques using experimental data from the CERN SRF model cavity. The study also explores the integration of sensing and actuation systems, including feedback mechanisms, to optimize noise control. The work has significant implications for the development of next-generation SRF cavities, which will play a crucial role in enabling the construction of future colliders. A new active learning strategy for deep learning models integrates both diversity and representativeness of the training data, using a specific metric to evaluate sample diversity and an adjusted margin threshold to account for the complexity of high-dimensional data. This approach ensures that the selected training samples effectively increase the model's knowledge, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through numerical experiments on image classification tasks. Additionally, we validate the proposed active learning strategy by applying it to real-world data sets and comparing its performance with existing methods based on distinct diversity and hardness criteria. Notably, the results show that our strategy outperforms the existing methods, even when using a basic margin threshold. This numerical evaluation is complemented by a case study illustrating the practical application of the proposed active learning strategy. Finally, we investigate the impact of sample diversity on the performance of active learning strategies, specifically for our strategy, and provide insights into its underlying behavior. This research is part of an ongoing investigation into the relationship between sample diversity and active learning. The validity of the Calderón-Zygmund theory in a bounded domain for the parabolic p-Laplacian system depends crucially on the smoothness of the coefficients. In particular, for constant coefficient parabolic systems, we demonstrate that a localized Calderón-Zygmund theory holds true in any bounded domain in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, provided that the coefficients exhibit smoothness at every point, except for a measure set with Hausdorff dimension less than n. This result is then extended to complex coefficients, where we find that a localized theory applies when the coefficients fall within the Sobolev space $W^{l,2}(\Omega)^m$, with $l>1-$, the Hausdorff dimension of singular points being less than $n$, and the coefficients satisfy a specific condition. Notably, these theorems remain applicable even in the case of coefficients belonging to $W^{1,2}(\Omega)^m$, a scenario previously considered unviable. The proof relies on the use of novel local $L^q$-weighted $W^{1,1}$ estimates. Consequently, we derive localized $L^q$-weighted Hörmander-type estimates for parabolic systems with complex coefficients, achieving the optimal level of smoothness. Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become a dominant approach in various fields, but its widespread adoption is hindered by federal data protection regulations.  Federated Reinforcement Learning (FRL), a variant of RL that trains agents on decentralized data while preserving confidentiality, has gained traction.  FRL differs from traditional RL in that agents not only learn from global policies but also share knowledge with clients.  This approach minimizes the need for data sharing and enhances policy transfer.  FRL has been applied to various tasks, including communication and game playing, and has shown superior performance compared to RL.  However, FRL's effectiveness is sensitive to several factors, including communication frequency, agent architecture, and training duration.  This review aims to provide an in-depth analysis of FRL's key aspects, including its benefits and drawbacks, current limitations, and future research directions.  The findings of this study are expected to provide valuable insights for researchers and practitioners working on FRL.  Furthermore, this review identifies open challenges and potential areas for future investigation within the field of FRL.  FRL's potential to improve RL's performance while maintaining data security is expected to lead to its increased adoption across various domains. between homogeneous elements that hold up under R-cohomological operations. 
Key results show that in a ring with characteristic zero, all relations in 
the c-differential spectrum can be expressed as power functions, and these power

discovery leads to a deeper understanding of power functions, and it provides a 
new basis for the free commutative ring in the context of c-differential

with characteristic zero, the ring's properties are completely determined by 
its unit group and the c-differential spectrum. Ultimately, the research 
demonstrates that the c-differential spectrum can be used to construct and 
investigate various ring properties. This work extends the understanding of 
commutative rings with zero characteristic and provides new insights into the 
structure of ring homology. Ultimately, the study sheds new light on ring 
homology and its applications in cohomology and stable homotopical invariants.

We define and examine the concept of $w_k$-equivalence for the category of welded string links, which is a broader generalization of classical string links. This investigation focuses on calculating $w_k$-equivalence classes of welded string links for various $k$, with the goal of formulating a unified theory for welded string links that builds upon Schubert's theorem for regular string links. To this end, we derive a set of comprehensive invariants based on Kauffman's skein algebra and then prove their invariance through a series of combinatorial and spectral sequence calculations. Ultimately, these findings contribute to the development of a unified theory for welded string links. This work also provides a comprehensive description of the Kauffman bracket skein module for welded string links in the solid torus, and it further generalizes previously established results for regular string links. Moreover, this research demonstrates the invariance of $w_k$-equivalence under isotopy for welded string links when $k$ is any integer value. To achieve this, we employ a novel method of spectral sequence calculation to analyze the algebraic structure of Kauffman's skein algebra and show that its generators can be used to compute $w_k$-equivalence classes for any $k$. Finally, this research also provides a comprehensive description of the Kauffman bracket skein module for welded string links in the solid torus, generalizing previously established results for regular string links. The active inference framework has been applied to various decision-making scenarios, 
where it reinterprets reward functions and optimizes them to achieve an optimal 
solution. In this paper, it is argued that active inference offers a unique 
approach to reward-based decision-making, where traditional reward functions are not necessary. 
Key to this argument is the derivation of a free energy equation under the assumption 
of a stationary prior over policies in environments characterized by stochastic systems 
with nonlinear dynamics and Gaussian noise. This derivation holds for both discrete and continuous action spaces, 
and it is demonstrated that active inference can be applied to both reinforcement learning and POMDP problems. 
To illustrate this, a modified version of the Cartpole problem is presented, 
in which no explicit reward function is used to train the policy. 
Instead, the policy is optimized to minimize an estimated free energy value, 
which is calculated from data generated by the policy. 
The results show that active inference can train a policy that achieves a near-optimal solution, 
as evaluated using the number of steps required to achieve a pole angle angle of ± 0.2. 
This work provides a novel perspective on decision-making in reinforcement learning and POMDP problems. 
It also provides a method for training policies without explicit reward functions, 
which may be useful in situations where reward functions are not available or difficult to estimate.

Overlap cycles are a type of Gray code, and we develop two distinct methods for creating them. Our initial approach involves overlap cycles generated from run-length codes, while the second method is derived from reflecting specific overlap codes. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to create overlap cycles for any length n from these generated codes, provided n is greater than or equal to m > 2. Examples are provided for both constructions. Additionally, we show how these overlap cycles can be utilized to construct a Gray code for lexicographically ordered sequences with specified overlap counts. Our results are compared to existing methods, and conclusions are drawn about potential further research opportunities. Lastly, we address a related open question posed in a previously published study. This research is based on previously unpublished work. This research introduces a groundbreaking You Only Hear Once (YOHO) approach to enhance the efficiency of audio event classification. By utilizing a single neural network that processes spectrograms, YOHO outperforms the conventional frame-based classification method, achieving notable speed improvements. YHO's speed gain is significantly due to the efficient processing of spectrograms in comparison to individual time frames. The study presents a novel spectrogram representation, called YOHO spectrograms, which significantly reduce redundancy and improve the model's speed and accuracy. The proposed YHO spectrograms are constructed by dividing each spectrogram into a set of smaller, random segments, each representing a set of frames, and then combining these segments into a single, more compact representation. The study demonstrates that YOHO spectrograms can be seamlessly integrated into the model without compromising the model's performance. The proposed approach is validated through extensive experiments on the popular ESC-50 and UBMC datasets, achieving state-of-the-art results in terms of speed and accuracy. This study introduces novel datasets for the Tatar language, comprising Tatar Text Classification and Tatar Named Entity Recognition. The introduced datasets are the first and only ones of their kind, featuring adapted categories for English Text Classification and adapted tags for English Named Entity Recognition. The Tatar Text Classification dataset comprises 10 large categories and 5 smaller ones, totaling 10,000 manually annotated examples, while the Tatar Named Entity recognition dataset features 12 prevalent tags and 5 less common ones, totaling 7,885 manually annotated examples. Both datasets were created using a mix of modern news articles, historical texts, and online resources, ensuring a balanced representation of Tatar language varieties. The datasets will be made publicly available through GitHub, allowing researchers to train, test, and evaluate NLP-compliant models for the Tatar language. The introduction of these datasets is crucial for training NLP models that can be applied in real-world applications related to the Tatar language, particularly in education, law, and information technology. Both datasets and the relevant code will be made available at https://github.com/ilnugumanov/tatar_nlp_datasets. Further information can be found at xalqaro.info. Deep learning techniques heavily rely on two key components: deep linear networks and self-attention mechanisms. However, optimizing the latter often leads to increased computational costs due to quadratic complexity, which can be a limitation for large datasets. To mitigate this issue, we introduce DAE-Former, a new attention mechanism that efficiently combines the strengths of deep linear networks and self-attention while reducing computational overhead. By leveraging the principle of duality, DAE-Former transforms the computation of self-attention into solving a difference of Euclidean distances optimization problem, which can be solved efficiently using semismooth Newton-type methods and linear network layers. This approach allows for the use of deep linear networks to approximate self-attention, resulting in a significant reduction in computational complexity. DAE-Former outperforms traditional self-attention mechanisms in both accuracy and speed, and its benefits can be observed across various applications, including image classification and semantic segmentation. Notably, DAE-Former achieves better results than traditional self-attention methods on large datasets, such as ImageNet and CIFAR-100, while requiring fewer parameters. Understanding how proteins interact is crucial for predicting the functions of unknown proteins and identifying the underlying processes that are disrupted by viral infections. By analyzing the similarities in the patterns of protein interactions, we can identify the key processes that are affected by a virus, which can help researchers understand how the virus functions and how it might be combated. In this research, we have developed a new method to measure the similarities in protein interactions using Bayesian inference. We tested this method using data from three different viruses on a large-scale protein network containing information about nearly 300 viral proteins and over 3,500 human proteins. The results show that our approach is more effective than other methods in identifying the key processes that are disrupted by the virus, and it can provide insights that are consistent with existing knowledge about the virus. Overall, this research demonstrates the potential of analyzing protein interactions to understand the underlying processes that are involved in a virus's lifecycle. We have developed a novel approach that integrates self-injection locking and wavelength conversion to create a compact, low-power laser system capable of producing ultra-short pulses with a narrow spectrum. By utilizing this hybrid method, a compact neodymium-doped fiber laser is able to produce 1.9 GHz pulses that are 1.2 picoseconds in duration and have a bandwidth of 0.9 nanometers. This breakthrough is notable due to the substantial reduction in required optical power, approximately two orders of magnitude lower than previous methods. Despite this progress, the quality of these designs and the originality of the ideas they represent remain subpar. Results indicate that AI-generated designs can effectively support the creative process, and the originality of the ideas they represent is comparable to that of human-created designs. Interestingly, AI-generated designs often incorporated previously unseen elements that human designers had not considered. These findings suggest that AI-assisted design systems have the potential to significantly benefit the creative process, and further research is needed to fully explore their capabilities in this field. Research on human-robot collaboration is gaining momentum, with a focus on
co-manipulation where robots work alongside humans to achieve shared objectives.
However, achieving collaborative goals requires robots to potentially make contact
with humans, which can be perceived as disturbances. To address this, we suggest
a predictive control approach that minimizes disturbances to human collaborators
while allowing robots to effectively interact with their environment. This is
achieved by projecting the human's state in the robot's local coordinate system,
using a learned dynamics model to forecast the human's future state. This enables
the robot to make predictive adjustments to its movement, reducing the impact
of contact on the human. We tested our method in simulated scenarios and real-world
experiments involving a collaborative robotic arm interacting with a human arm.
The results show that our method significantly minimizes disturbances to the human
and the overall time taken to complete tasks, while also improving task efficiency
and success rates in both simulated and real-world settings. The code for our
method is publicly available at https://github.com/isaac-msr/robot-collaboration.

The evaluation of Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) models is typically based on accuracy scores, yet rare errors significantly skew results, causing the ranking of systems to be highly unreliable. To address this issue, we introduce RARE, a novel evaluation method that overcomes the limitations of traditional accuracy metrics. RARE categorizes GEC output into three categories - correct, common error, and rare error - and employs a hierarchical approach to assess the performance of models. The proposed method is demonstrated with four GEC systems, revealing that previous evaluations often unfairly penalized models on rare errors, where in fact the models were performing similarly on more frequent errors. Moreover, we find that rare error detection is a challenging task, suggesting that future research should focus on developing more accurate identification tools. The RARE evaluation method and supporting code are available at https://github.com/jykim96/rare. A Pytorch implementation of RARE is also provided for users to replicate our experiments. The corrected evaluation results for state-of-the-art GEC systems on the GUMTREE dataset are as follows: mteviL (82.8%), Figgyn (81.9), Copyme (78.8), and CMBEXT (80.1). The prevalence of dead pixels on imaging devices necessitates research into dead pixel classification, a crucial step in improving future applications. We utilize convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to classify dead pixels based on single images and find that dead pixel representation affects model performance. We examine how CNNs respond to training with and without dead pixel labels and discover that incorporating dead pixel labels during training slightly enhances generalization and classification accuracy. Notably, when omitting dead pixel labels, the network is still able to accurately classify and locate dead pixels, suggesting that the information from live pixels is sufficient to learn and recognize dead pixel patterns. We also find that dead pixel distribution has a negligible impact on generalization and classification performance. Furthermore, we discover that dead pixel classification is influenced by the surrounding pixel values, a relationship that can be exploited to improve classification results. We also investigate the effect of dead pixel distribution and density on classification performance, concluding that dead pixel density has a negligible impact on classification accuracy, although the distribution of dead pixels does have a significant effect. Notably, we find that dead pixel density does not correlate with classification performance, suggesting that dead pixel distribution is a more significant factor in predicting pixel death. Our study provides new insights into dead pixel classification, the behavior of CNNs in response to dead pixel labels, and the factors influencing dead pixel classification, including pixel density and distribution. We also present a new approach for dead pixel classification that leverages the spatial distribution of dead pixels to improve classification accuracy. Our findings are expected to inform the development of future imaging devices with improved dead pixel performance. We introduce AppealNet, a novel approach that dynamically controls the trade-off between the accuracy and computational efficiency of deep learning models by selectively activating their layers during execution. To achieve this, AppealNet estimates the accuracy gain of each layer and compares it to its associated computational cost, then uses a dynamic threshold to decide whether to activate each layer or skip it. AppealNet's model threshold determination process is streamlined by utilizing a cost-accuracy mapping technique, which approximates the accuracy loss due to omitting activation of a layer and its subsequent impact on subsequent layers. This process is integrated into the model training, allowing AppealNet to optimize its performance without additional inference overhead. Our evaluation of AppealNet on ResNet-50 and MobileNetV2 demonstrates its ability to match the accuracy of full-precision models while significantly reducing inference costs, with ResNet-50 achieving 99.9% accuracy at a cost of 19% of its full precision counterpart and MobileNetV2 reaching 94.8% accuracy at 78% of its original cost. We investigated the orbital evolution of the sub-Jovian planet HD 167768 b in a hierarchical system consisting of a low-mass star and a companion star. Utilizing Gaia's early third data release, we found the system to have an orbital period of approximately 2,700 days. By applying the MESA stellar evolution code, we determined the evolution history of the host star and its companion, leading us to conclude that HD 167768 b will likely become a hot Jupiter within the next billion years. Consequently, the planet is an excellent candidate for current and future surveys to capture during close approaches. Notably, the planet's orbital eccentricity is predicted to be around 0.10, making it detectable through the Doppler effect via high-resolution spectroscopy. Moreover, the planet's orbital dynamics are expected to lead to tidal dissipation in its host star, potentially producing detectable signatures through the laser cooling technique. Ultimately, HD 167768 b presents an exciting opportunity to explore the planet's orbital evolution through observations and simulations. PEEL, a novel pruning technique inspired by economic principles, optimizes neural networks by efficiently allocating resources. This method identifies critical layers and assigns them sufficient resources, reassessing non-essential layers to save them memory, thereby achieving a balanced network configuration. Furthermore, our framework was found to be robust in the presence of diverse client factors and varying levels of data imbalance. Additionally, our framework was shown to be effective in achieving fairness while allowing for the efficient use of communication resources in FL settings. The study involved human participants who worked alongside a machine to identify objects in a video stream, a task previously shown to elicit varying levels of trust. The study's findings also suggest that trust is influenced by the similarity between the machine's and operator's performance, particularly when humans are involved in the decision-making process. FlexMatch, a semi-supervised learning algorithm, combines pseudo-labeling with a flexible approach to unlabelled data by dynamically adjusting the confidence threshold based on class probability distributions. Unlike traditional methods like FixMatch and Mean-Teacher, FlexMatch doesn't require predefined threshold values or a single confidence threshold across the entire training process. Instead, FlexMatch adjusts the threshold for each data point to maximize the accuracy of its predicted class. We evaluate FlexMatch's effectiveness on the SVHN and CIFAR-10/100 datasets and show that it outperforms existing algorithms, achieving notable improvements of 2.1%, 2.5%, and 0.3% on average precision for the respective datasets. FlexMatch's source code is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/riquetong/FlexMatch. Furthermore, FlexMatch can be adapted for multi-task learning scenarios where the training data is shared across multiple classification tasks. We demonstrate this capability by applying FlexMatch to a dataset containing images with multiple labels and show that the algorithm can effectively learn to identify a wide range of classifiable data points. Additionally, FlexMatch's dynamic threshold adjustment can be guided by a user-defined confidence threshold, enabling the algorithm to prioritize the creation of high-confidence pseudo-labels for specific classes. We illustrate this capability by applying FlexMatch to a dataset where the algorithm is constrained to produce high-confidence pseudo-labels for a specific set of labels, while still learning to identify other classifiable data points. We validate FlexMatch's effectiveness in this multi-task setting by comparing it with state-of-the-art algorithms and evaluating its performance on the specific labels of interest. The results show that FlexMatch achieves state-of-the-art performance on the specific labels, while still learning to identify other classifiable data points efficiently. We demonstrate FlexMatch's effectiveness on the CIFAR-10/100 datasets and show that the algorithm can achieve state-of-the-art performance on the specific labels, which is 2.1%, 2.5%, and 0.3% higher than the existing baseline methods. The source code of FlexMatch is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/riquetong/FlexMatch. We also provide a supplementary video that visualizes the algorithm's threshold adjustment process in real-time at https://sites.google.com/view/flexmatch-paper/home/. In the context of federated learning, training a machine learning model for a multitude of clients requires balancing their unique privacy needs while keeping communication expenses in check. A common strategy is to employ a central server to coordinate communication among clients. However, this approach becomes impractical when the number of clients is large due to scalability issues. To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach, pFedHN, which combines local model parallelization with horizontal partitioning to minimize communication costs. By dividing data into segments and processing them separately, pFedHN reduces communication requirements during the computation and gradient combination phases of the training process. Furthermore, pFedHN is a straightforward adaptation of existing federated learning techniques, such as federated linear regression and federated linear regression with regularization, and can be applied to other models. Our experiments demonstrate that pFedHN achieves comparable accuracy to centralized methods while reducing communication costs. Moreover, pFedHN outperforms decentralized learning techniques, such as federated averaging, by achieving higher accuracy for a large number of clients. When dealing with non-convex problems, pFedHN is shown to converge to a stable point, even in the presence of adversarial attacks. Our experiments also reveal that pFedHN is resistant to non-IID data distributions and can achieve comparable accuracy to centralized methods in such scenarios. Overall, pFedHN is a versatile approach that can be applied to a range of federated learning techniques, making it a promising solution for real-world applications. Multilingual language models are trained on text from various languages to develop the ability to understand and analyze language. These models typically consist of a shared multilingual encoder and a language-independent task predictor. In this paper, we investigate the impact of fine-tuning on the components of multilingual language models, specifically focusing on multilingual BERT. We find that the multilingual encoder and the predictor are updated in different ways during the fine-tuning process, which can result in the model becoming less flexible. To address this, we propose a method to fine-tune both components simultaneously. We also find that the multilingual encoder continues to learn from the data during fine-tuning, which can lead to the model being biased towards the language of the training data. To mitigate this, we recommend using ensembles of multiple multilingual models trained on different data sources. These ensembles can be trained in two ways: either by fine-tuning a single model on multiple data sources or by training an ensemble of models separately. We also propose a method to combine the predictions of multiple models in the ensemble. Our experiments on the NER task, which involves text classification across multiple languages, demonstrate that our proposed methods can lead to significant improvements in the accuracy of the model. Specifically, we show that the ensemble model can achieve a high accuracy of 89.5% compared to the baseline model that was trained on a single language, which only managed to achieve an accuracy of 85.1%. A software project's vulnerability assessment is often confined to its own code, overlooking how external library dependencies contribute to its susceptibility.
To address this limitation, we have developed a method to calculate the risk associated with a project's library, taking into account the vulnerabilities found in those third-party libraries.
We applied this approach to assess the vulnerability risk of nearly 10,000 Python projects across their most-used packages, discovering that nearly a quarter of these projects are at high risk due to shared vulnerabilities among their library dependencies.
The results demonstrate the value of this approach, enabling the identification of projects with similar levels of vulnerability in their library portfolios, thus facilitating targeted, efficient, and comprehensive vulnerability assessments. Accident Prediction in Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) is a critical issue that has garnered significant research attention. Existing methods primarily employ spatio-temporal models to forecast accidents, yet they struggle with the limitations of lacking spatial and temporal context. To address this, we present the Dynamic Spatial-Temporal Attention (DSTA) network, which integrates a graph neural network and a self-attention mechanism. By establishing a dynamic attention graph, DSTA dynamically selects key nodes and links to focus on accident-prone areas and routes, ultimately enhancing accident prediction accuracy. Our experimental results indicate that DSTA significantly surpasses existing approaches, achieving a 6.6% improvement in overall accuracy and 8.9% in route accuracy. Moreover, DSTA's performance is further validated through a case study, which demonstrates its potential for real-world applications. A recent breakthrough in memory management, version-based reclamation (VBR), outperforms previous optimistic methods, which often struggle with unbounded memory usage and guarantee violations. This innovative approach uses a graph-based algorithm to safely recover versioned objects with a guaranteed time complexity, outshining existing non-optimistic methods, despite lacking composability. We present two new extensions of VBR that maintain its advantages: a modified VBR, which ensures linearity while offering better performance, and a multi-level VBR, which enables the management of more complex data structures with reduced overhead. Through experimentation, we observed significant improvements in both systems, which consistently outperformed other similar systems, with only a minimal increase in memory usage. The modified VBR and multi-level VBR are part of the Hemera runtime system, which has been made publicly available for testing purposes. Image restoration, a complex task involving multiple challenges, is addressed in this research by leveraging the properties of low-rank Hankel matrices within a two-stage model. Initially, a method is developed to estimate the underlying rank from a single measurement, then the collaborative sparse model is employed to estimate the coefficients of the Hankel matrix, which are subsequently used to calculate the restored image. Due to the non-convex nature of the problem, a hybrid approach involving sparse optimization and regression is utilized to obtain an analytical solution for the image restoration. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed two-stage approach's ability to handle significant measurement degradations, outperforming existing methods for image restoration. Additionally, a theoretical analysis is provided, and the underlying principles are generalized to tackle multi-image recovery in the presence of motion. An image deblurring example is presented, where the proposed method successfully restores images from severely degraded conditions involving both motion and blurring. The underlying principles are further generalized to tackle the more complex multi-image recovery problem in the presence of motion. The development of autonomous driving systems relies heavily on understanding complex human behavior. To improve the analysis of pedestrian actions, a hybrid learning approach combining a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) network and a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is proposed. This approach enables the classification of different pedestrian crossing actions, such as stopping, looking back, throwing objects, and crossing, among others. Using data from the Caltech Datasets, a comparative analysis was conducted between the proposed hybrid model and a standard CNN. Experimental results showed that the hybrid model outperformed the CNN with accuracy rates of 93.64% and 86.67% respectively. These findings indicate that the hybrid approach offers a more accurate and efficient method for analyzing and predicting pedestrian crossing actions. Ultimately, this approach has the potential to enhance autonomous driving systems by predicting the actions of pedestrians at pedestrian crossings. We develop a quality-focused MTC strategy that estimates the received power distribution at Type-II MTCs and enables Type-I devices to adjust their transmission probabilities based on the estimated channel quality indicator (CQI) values. identification of high-potential images that can be restored to their original 
form, significantly improving overall image quality. Experimental results show 
that our method, trained solely on high-quality images, can enhance the 
restoration potential in a wide range of dynamic scenes, outperforming existing 
methods in image quality prediction. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness 
of our image quality prediction model on low-quality images captured by real-world 
cameras under various conditions. Our code and dataset are available online.

and demonstrates its potential in a variety of applications. The restoration 
potential of an image can be used to guide the capture of high-quality images, 
improve image editing, and enhance image synthesis. We are making our dataset

We have developed a theory of Galois coverings on tropical curves that satisfies properties of functoriality, transitivity, and Galois connectivity. Specifically, we have derived detailed constraints for the composition of such coverings and their branching indices. Moreover, we have demonstrated that the associated sheet counts adhere to a modified version of Hurwitz's theorem when composed in a sequence. Ultimately, we have applied our framework to investigate Galois coverings in the context of a non-Archimedean field's valuation space. This work draws upon fundamental concepts in Galois theory and geometric techniques, with notable influences from Birman and Zamolodchikov. Our research also builds upon existing theories of hyperbolic coverings by Lima, Yang, and Kato. This paper presents a novel approach to Bayesian transfer learning, which involves determining the probability distribution of the target function's true value. By leveraging this method, we can more accurately estimate the target function's true value and its associated uncertainty, which is crucial for reliable classification. Our approach, dubbed optimal Bayesian transfer learning, not only provides more accurate results but also enables the comparison of classification error in different domains without requiring target function information. Our findings, validated through experiments on both simulated and real-world data, demonstrate the efficacy of our method and highlight its advantages over existing transfer learning methods. Moreover, our approach offers a practical solution for estimating the target function's true value in classification problems. Finally, we outline promising areas of future research that hold potential for further advancements in Learned Index technology. Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have garnered significant attention due to their potential to mimic the biological workings of the human brain, with notable advancements in performance on benchmark tasks such as MNIST and CIFAR-10. However, SNNs still lag behind conventional deep learning networks in terms of accuracy. This disparity stems from fundamental differences in the training and evaluation mechanisms of SNNs and conventional neural networks, with the former being more susceptible to noise due to their event-driven nature. To address this issue, we introduce a novel noise injection technique that enhances SNN performance on classification tasks. Specifically, we create a noise injection module that mimics the noise patterns observed in sensory neurons and can be applied dynamically during training. When activated, this module generates stochastic inputs to SNNs during training, with the goal of enhancing their robustness to noise. To evaluate the efficacy of this approach, we conducted experiments on two benchmark datasets - CIFAR-10B and ImageNet - with our SNN models exhibiting a substantial boost in performance compared to their noise-free counterparts. Notably, the proposed noise injection technique can be easily adapted to a wide range of SNN applications, with the code available for public access. This contribution offers a new pathway for refining the training and evaluation processes of SNNs, with the potential to accelerate the development of more accurate and efficient models. The corresponding code can be accessed at https://github.com/taoancai2001/NoiseInjection. A 64-bit binary for the NoiseInjection model has also been made available for users to run on their own hardware. map, which is then combined with user-annotated proposals to produce the final 
segmentation result. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms

We provide an alternative proof of the renormalized system theorem that links preparatory properties with algebraic characteristics of the renormalized system, thereby establishing a connection between the renormalized trace and the trace on the algebra of observables in classical mechanics. This connection is further explored in a companion study that generalizes the theory to quantum mechanics, where we develop a renormalized trace on the algebra of quantum observables and prove that it satisfies the Schatten norm vanishing condition for the Schrödinger renormalized system. Our approach builds upon prior research by Buzzi and Demmel, and we also derive a new formula for the Schatten norm of the Schrödinger renormalized system using the conjugacy map between formal and Borel measures on the complex plane. As an application, we show that the Schatten norm of the Schrödinger renormalized system is zero if and only if the limit of the Borel norm of the renormalized system is zero, and we also establish a new formula for the Borel norm of the Schrödinger renormalized system in terms of the convergent subsequence of the Birkhoff transform. Go is gaining widespread acceptance as a top-notch systems programming language due to its ability to write robust, efficient, and reliable programs. However, like any concurrent systems programming language, Go is prone to bugs resulting from data races. Current approaches for detecting concurrency issues in Go applications have significant limitations: they require source code to be recompiled, can only identify specific types of bugs, and are not suitable for production environments. Our research introduces GoRPM, a runtime detection system that runs on standard Go RPM packages, uses statistical analysis to detect concurrency issues, and can be easily integrated into existing Go applications. GoRPM has successfully identified 99% of the known concurrency problems tested, exceeding the performance of existing runtime detection tools. GoRPM is now available as an open-source tool for researchers and developers to use. Additionally, we have conducted an in-depth empirical study to demonstrate the effectiveness of GoRPM under various scenarios, including real-world applications and large-scale distributed environments. Our study confirms that GoRPM is a reliable and efficient method for detecting concurrency issues in Go applications. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have been applied to various chemistry and material science tasks, including predicting quantum properties. A key challenge in these problems is that standard attention mechanisms, which consider the importance of connections between atoms, are insufficient because they treat all bonds equally without considering their direction. This directionality issue is particularly problematic when analyzing cyclic molecules. In this study, we introduce the Equiformer, a message-passing graph neural network that utilizes complex numbers to encode bond directionality. The Equiformer is capable of learning complex transformations, including complex rotations, and can be applied to both directed and undirected graphs. We demonstrate the benefits of the Equiformer through its improved performance on the Quantum Chemistry Benchmarks (QCB) dataset, and its ability to make more accurate predictions for cyclic molecules. Furthermore, we show that the Equiformer's learned transformations can be applied to other related tasks, such as predicting molecular orbitals. The source code for the Equiformer is publicly available on GitHub. We also present theoretical analysis of the Equiformer's behavior using tools from noncommutative Fourier analysis. This work highlights the potential of complex-valued graph neural networks for solving graph-based problems that require directional information. As complex-valued deep learning models become more widely used, we anticipate that the Equiformer's unique design may inspire new applications in machine learning. The source code for the Equiformer is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/DeepQuantum/equiformer. Additional information and results are available at https://deepquantum.github.io/equiformer/. Supplemental materials, including the source code and additional results, can be found at https://nrg-seokhyeon.github.io/equiformer/. In future work, we plan to explore the use of noncommutative Fourier analysis to study the Equiformer's learned transformations in more detail. We introduce Multiverse, a novel deep learning framework for predicting movement trajectories in scenarios where accurate predictions are hindered by uncertainty in future conditions. Drawing inspiration from cosmology, we develop the Multiverse model to generate a range of plausible future trajectories for each trajectory to be predicted, allowing multiple potential outcomes to be represented in a probabilistic manner. Our framework incorporates a dynamic set of future states, whose distribution across multiple generations is controlled by a learnable scaling factor. This model can be trained using different loss functions, including one that maximizes the dynamic coverage of the predicted distributions. Our evaluation of the Multiverse model on real-world datasets from various domains, including human activity, air traffic, and ocean buoy monitoring, demonstrates its ability to effectively represent a range of future scenarios and achieve superior results compared to established methods. The resulting controller can also operate effectively in real-time, making it suitable for a variety of applications. In the context of online learning with regret, we investigate a scenario where a learner repeatedly selects actions from a compact space, receiving immediate feedback in the form of real-valued losses after each selection. The actions and associated losses are drawn from a compact space and possess certain structural properties, including Lipschitz continuity for the objective function and a bounded diameter for the set of actions. Under these conditions, we establish a learning rate bound that scales inversely with the chosen step-size, and one that is also bounded by the square root of the Poincaré constant associated with the action set. Building on this framework, we extend it to encompass more complex structural assumptions, including those related to convexity, local Lipschitz continuity, and Lipschitz continuity with respect to a norm. To illustrate the applicability of our results, we provide multiple examples, including online optimization with a regularized regret bound, robust least-squares regression, and stochastic online low-rank matrix factorization. The underlying analysis is grounded in a novel application of the Bellman gradient method, and a novel approach to analyzing regret bounds in the context of non-convex settings. Additionally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a range of numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. We introduce DLSpec, a Distributed Learning (DL) framework designed for large-scale deep learning tasks, specifically tailored for large neural networks. The DL framework allows for distributed training across multiple machines, using a shared parameter space to facilitate model synchronization. The key challenge in distributed training lies in balancing the exchange of updated parameters, particularly for large neural networks where synchronization can be a major bottleneck. To address this issue, DLSpec employs a novel approach, leveraging a hierarchical model representation to break up large neural networks into smaller units, such as layers. Each machine within the DL environment then trains a subset of these units, minimizing communication costs by limiting the exchange of parameters. The integration of DLSpec with PyTorch enables seamless support for multiple distributed data storage solutions, such as HDFS and S3, facilitating DL system deployment on various cloud platforms. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of DLSpec in significantly enhancing the scalability of DL tasks, particularly for large neural networks. Notably, DLSpec outperforms other state-of-the-art DL systems, such as HDFS and S3, in training tasks such as image recognition and language modeling, with a notable improvement in training time. Quantum machine learning has the potential to solve complex tasks that traditional machine learning finds difficult. However, it remains unclear if quantum machine learning outperforms classical approaches on simpler problems that are already solvable classically. We conducted a thorough comparison of the effectiveness of quantum machine learning on basic tasks, specifically binary classification, regression, and clustering, using various algorithms and datasets. The results showed that quantum machine learning performed similarly to classical approaches on these initial datasets but outshone it on a more intricate variant of a problem called a magnetic protein sequence classification task. Furthermore, our experiment revealed that the level of complexity of the data significantly impacts the performance of quantum machine learning, with some data sets benefiting more from its capabilities than others. We also investigated the influence of data distribution and dimensionality, discovering that quantum machine learning can handle data that classical algorithms struggle with due to their inherent limitations. Overall, our study suggests that quantum machine learning can provide advantages in handling intricate problems but may not significantly improve classical approaches on simpler tasks. We propose that future research focus on developing tasks that are truly challenging for classical algorithms in order to accurately assess the true potential of quantum machine learning. A novel receiver design is proposed for sparse code multiple access based on the variational autoencoder (VAE) technique. The VAE model is trained to predict the sparse active codeword of SCMA given the received signal, outperforming existing methods that rely on solving an optimization problem. Specifically, we integrate the receiver into a system that uses recursive group sparse modeling and deep learning-based sparse code multiple access, which employs a renormalization group approach to reduce the complexity of SCMA. The results demonstrate that this integrated system achieves lower bit error rates and simplified decoding, as well as significantly reduced complexity at the receiver. Additionally, the proposed design allows for efficient expansion to multi-user multiple-input single-output and multi-user multiple-input multiple-output systems, which is not feasible with previous methods. Our results also show that this approach can be extended to an MMSE detector in MMWave-MIMO and eMMSE detector in eMMSE-MIMO systems. This study explores the challenge of allocating resources to achieve optimal social welfare in dynamic networks that consist of interacting agents. Unlike typical welfare optimization problems, we focus on equilibria here, as they are a more realistic reflection of the agents' behavior compared to centralized solutions. To this end, we demonstrate that a competitive equilibrium effectively maximizes social welfare within the confines of key environmental and technological constraints. Additionally, we develop a novel approach for computing equilibria in these networks and show its effectiveness through both theoretical and empirical analysis. Our algorithm is versatile and can be applied to a broader range of problems beyond resource allocation, including the scheduling of agents and the distribution of resources for network flow optimization. Moreover, we present a simplified model for efficient resource allocation and validate its practicality by applying it to real-world data from the NFL schedule. Lastly, we highlight the potential benefits and challenges of implementing our algorithms in dynamic networks and outline avenues for future research. This paper presents a novel, iterative approach to calculating 3D motion paths from 2D feature tracks, enhancing the process of obtaining viewing graphs from 3D trajectory data. By iteratively updating both the 3D path and 2D feature pairings, our method surpasses traditional viewing graph computation methods, which rely on pre-computed 3D motion paths. Our study explores how hydrogen affects the electronic properties of the silicide $\beta$-Si$_2$Al, which is a model system for understanding metal-hydrogen interactions. We found that the adsorption of hydrogen on the (100) surface of $\beta$-Si$_2$Al leads to a significant modification of the electronic structure, which is characterized by the formation of new energy bands. These energy bands exhibit a high degree of dispersion near the Fermi level and are likely driven by the formation of new interatomic bonds between silicon and aluminum atoms. Notably, the presence of hydrogen leads to a significant increase in the energy of electride electrons near the Fermi level, which is a unique phenomenon compared to other metal-hydrogen systems. Our findings suggest that the interaction between hydrogen and electride electrons may have a significant impact on the electronic properties of $\beta$-Si$_2$Al and could potentially explain the observed hydrogenation effects on the material's Fermi level. This discovery could provide new insights into the role of hydrogen in influencing the electronic properties of electride materials. A widely used statistical method involves creating a model to make predictions and then comparing these predictions to real-world data. This comparison often yields discrepancies, but the nature and significance of these discrepancies are often underdiscussed. We propose a new perspective on this process by viewing it as a Bayesian inference problem, focusing on modeling the model's shortcomings. This approach allows for a more detailed understanding of predictions and their discrepancies, revealing interesting properties, such as the distinction between unexpected events and random variations. We apply our method to data from a 2019 earthquake in California, showing how it can be used to quantify uncertainty in earthquake risk. This framework can be used to reframe traditional statistical modeling into a more comprehensive practice of 'data forking', where predictions are viewed as branches in a tree of possible outcomes, allowing for more accurate assessments of risk and probability. This new paradigm offers a more transparent and reliable way to make predictions, enabling the quantification of risk across multiple scenarios. Malware detection based on file attributes is a viable approach, but its effectiveness depends heavily on the attributes used. This research explores the potential of using statistical features of file contents for malware detection, specifically for identifying ransomware. By analyzing entropy characteristics of file contents, our study found significant differences between ransomware and legitimate files, indicating that ransomware typically exhibits lower entropy and a greater concentration of samples near zero on a probability scale. Our experiments utilizing the deep learning algorithm CapsNet showed promising results, with an accuracy rate of over 99%. Furthermore, our approach can be integrated with existing content-based detection methods. Although CapsNet's vulnerability to adversarial examples is a concern, our findings suggest that the use of probability distribution entropy as a feature may provide resilience against such attacks. Our research also highlights the need for further investigation into the underlying causes of ransomware encryption algorithms' behavior, as observed in this study. This research introduces a novel approach to depth estimation, referred to as center-aware depth encoding, where the primary goal is to enhance accuracy rather than optimize compression efficiency. The proposed method, based on center-aware depth encoding, involves a center-aware model and a refinement model that work in tandem to improve depth prediction accuracy. The center-aware model processes input images to yield depth predictions, which are then refined by the refinement model to produce a more precise output. Experimental results demonstrate that combining these two models can lead to significant accuracy gains, achieving a notable increase of over 1% in depth accuracy when compared to the state-of-the-art depth estimation methods, all while using a similar model size as efficient depth estimation networks like center-based and cascade-based models. The accompanying code is publicly available at https://github.com/IIITDJain/Center-Aware-Depth-Encoding. A qualitative comparison with the state-of-the-art depth estimation models is also provided at https://iiitj.org/80.

Our research focuses on disconnection within colloidal droplet suspensions as a percolation system, examining disconnection rates as droplets interact. This research introduces a novel method to enhance speaker localization in noisy environments using external microphone signals as a reference. We examine the capabilities of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with a focus on complex Taylor-Green problems featuring variable spatial dimensions. Our analysis reveals that PINN performance is notably hindered when higher-order complexities such as additional equations or enlarged time domains are introduced. Furthermore, we observe that PINNs struggle with the ground truth of the Taylor-Green problem in higher-order instances, which is attributed to increased model complexities. Additionally, we explore the potential of incorporating a spectral normalization layer into the PINN architecture to enhance its representational capabilities and, consequently, its accuracy. Our findings suggest that incorporating this layer can yield improved accuracy, particularly in the complex Taylor-Green problem setting. The results of our study are expected to provide valuable insights for the practical application of PINNs in solving PDEs. The rapid growth of video content and mobile devices has led to an increase in data consumption, making it challenging for service providers to balance quality, capacity, and cost. To address this issue, a new video compression system called Gemino is introduced. Gemino enhances the efficiency of existing video codecs by reorganizing video frames and incorporating viewer attention to achieve better video quality at lower bitrates. The system's encoder reorganizes video data based on its importance and estimated viewer attention, while the decoder uses this structure to prioritize frames for display. Gemino's decoder calculates viewer attention based on pixel characteristics and adapts the display order of frames accordingly, ensuring that critical parts of the video are shown even at low bitrates. Evaluation of Gemino shows that it significantly improves video quality, achieving up to 9.5 dB better PSNR compared to traditional codecs at very low bitrates, making it an ideal solution for streaming services. The system's source and decoder are made available under an open-source license to promote further research. Gemino's effectiveness is demonstrated through its successful deployment on a major video sharing platform, achieving a significant 50% reduction in required bitrate while maintaining high video quality. The system's impact on the platform was evaluated using a real-world test involving 1.2 billion video views. More details about the system, including its code and test results, can be found at https://gemino.vncp.cs.cmu.edu/. By integrating this policy with a manipulation controller, the manipulation system achieves significantly improved results. Our policy optimization yields a notable enhancement, with a 3.5 times increase in success rate when manipulating garments on a human body, accomplished through the same set of actions. Our proposed system can be applied to a range of tasks such as adjusting the fit, adding decorations, and orienting garments in space. Additionally, we showcase the potential of adapting our system to a more efficient manipulation method with a single action. In India, a land of many languages, a diverse range of languages exists with varying levels of resource availability. The languages of Bihar and Jharkhand in the eastern part of India - such as Bhojpuri, Magahi, and Maithili - fall in between well-resourced Hindi and tribal languages. Given their mutual intelligibility, these languages can potentially benefit from shared resources. This work explores the feasibility of this by comparing the performance of language identification and sentiment analysis models for these languages, using both shared and separate training methods. Our results show that using separate training data achieves better performance for these languages, but using shared training methods results in surprisingly good performance at a low data requirement. This achievement is attributed to the development of a new dataset for sentiment analysis in these languages, a first of its kind. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the need for more advanced Maithili language technology. All the used datasets and code are openly accessible at a specified GitHub repository.

A key goal is to create a system that can learn from unique situations and quickly forget irrelevant information. A proposed approach utilizes a memory-based model, where past data is represented as discrete points with weights reflecting their importance. A dynamic forgetting mechanism is incorporated, allowing weights to be adjusted to balance learning from new observations and forgetting unnecessary information. A novel algorithm, the Weighted Transitions Algorithm (WTA), is developed to implement this mechanism. The algorithm's performance is evaluated on various navigation tasks, including the MDP Framework, where it demonstrates the ability to achieve optimal solutions and efficiently forget unnecessary information. The effectiveness of WTA is further illustrated through experiments on the classic gridworld domain. The results show that WTA outperforms a baseline model, which does not incorporate forgetting, and exhibits more efficient information retention. The proposed algorithm is suitable for practical applications and can be implemented in real-time, making it a viable solution for autonomous vehicle navigation. We have developed a novel, high-performance method for mapping out the fermion subspace on an infinite-range boson model, specifically the Bose-Hubbard model. By incorporating a fermion-boson transformation, we've created a more efficient mapping technique that yields significantly improved results. Our approach results in a substantial 8 to 100-fold reduction in the number of qubits required for simulation compared to previous methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on a system of $N$ sites with an average of $\mu N$ fermions, showing that it can be simulated with a constant number of qubits. Our results also show that dynamic systems can be efficiently simulated, with a cost scaling with the number of time steps and the number of fermions at the end state. We further show that our method can be used to simulate systems with a finite average number of fermions, with a cost that scales sublinearly with $N$. These results demonstrate the potential of our mapping technique to simulate large fermion systems on current quantum hardware. Our work paves the way for the simulation of quantum many-body systems with a variable number of particles, with implications for the study of quantum phase transitions and many-body physics. This study investigates the use of vision transformers (ViTs) for generating bird's eye view (BEV) maps, a novel application that contrasts ViTs' current BEV map generation capabilities, which are derived from convolutional neural networks (CNNs). We discovered that ViTs can produce accurate BEV maps without relying on convolutional operations, which are typically required for object detection in depth camera images. However, ViTs struggle to maintain their performance in object detection tasks, which we attribute to their inability to utilize local spatial information efficiently in detection contexts. To overcome this limitation, we developed a framework that integrates spatial attention and a hierarchical encoding scheme for creating high-quality BEV maps, which we found to be challenging for ViTs to replicate using traditional methods. The results of our experiments, which were conducted using the Waymo Open dataset, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, which we have made publicly available on GitHub. This study addresses the challenge of anomaly detection, where the system must identify samples from classes it has not seen before. A novel solution, the Out-of-distribution Pseudo-Gaussian method (OPG), generates artificial samples resembling known classes but with Gaussian distributions. These synthetic samples are then used to train an adapted Gaussian mixture classifier, which combines these artificial samples with real samples from known classes. During testing, the classifier is presented with real samples from both seen and unseen classes, and it distinguishes between them by comparing probabilities. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of OPG in outperforming established anomaly detection techniques, both in terms of accuracy and resource efficiency. Additionally, the method exhibits resilience in scenarios where training data is limited, and it performs significantly better than existing methods in these conditions. A key benefit of OPG lies in its ability to handle unseen classes without the need for extensive parameter tuning or modifications to the underlying classifier. Traditional piecewise stationary time series models are commonly used to address correlations within datasets and are composed of multiple segments with distinct parameters, each representing different periods of stationarity. However, these models often fail to capture dependencies between segment transitions and may be ineffective in real-world applications where abrupt changes are rare. To address this issue, we propose a new model, the piecewise stationary augmented linear drift (PSALD) model, which enables a more nuanced understanding of complex time series data. By incorporating a stochastic process to govern segment transitions, we can better account for subtle changes in the underlying data. We derive the PSALD model's joint distribution and develop a maximum likelihood estimation method for parameter optimization, while also demonstrating its asymptotic properties. Furthermore, we show that the PSALD model can handle a broader range of dependence patterns and is more flexible than traditional piecewise stationary models. Through simulation studies and real-world applications, we demonstrate the PSALD model's effectiveness in handling large datasets and achieving superior performance compared to other models. Finally, we provide code for implementing the PSALD model in supplementary materials. These materials are available online at https://github.com/ChenDong2018/PSALD.
